That's a great question to sit with, and I want to say plainly: you're not missing something obvious, and your friend isn't crazy to notice it. Jesus really doesn't walk around saying the bare words "I am God." But it helps to ask why a first-century Jew would never say that so casually. As one line of evidence in this study puts it, Israel's world was shaped by the Shema — "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD" (Deuteronomy 6:4) — a "jealous, boundaried monotheism for which Jews had died." In that world, saying "I am God" outright would sound like either madness or blasphemy, and it would flatten the very thing Jesus is revealing: that he is God as the Son, distinct from the Father, not a second deity or an interchangeable label.

So instead of the bare claim, Jesus uses language that, read against that Jewish background, says something even more precise. "Before Abraham was, I am" deliberately echoes the divine Name; being called "the First and the Last," "the I AM," receiving worship, and being enthroned "with the Ancient of Days" are, as the case is laid out, "Old Testament identifiers of the God of Israel, deliberately laid upon Jesus of Nazareth." These aren't vaguer than "I am God" — they're the fingerprint of the divine identity given through a title, "Son of God," that preserves his personal relation to the Father while still placing him inside that identity.

The clearest confirmation comes not from Jesus' own lips but from how he receives others' confessions. When Thomas falls before the risen Christ and says "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28), Jesus does not correct him — he blesses him and everyone who will believe on that same testimony. If Jesus were merely the Son in some lesser sense, accepting that worship would be, as the introduction to this whole case states, not a misunderstanding but blasphemy. So "Son of God" isn't a demotion from "God" — in John's Gospel it's the very title that unpacks, in Jewish terms, what it means for the eternal Word, distinct in person from the Father, to be truly God become man.
